Rain warning begins in England and Wales as Storm Boelo hits UK
Summary
Storm Boelo is bringing more wet and windy weather to large parts of the UK - a day after
Storm Austen hit the country
A yellow warning for rain began at
11:00 in large parts of England and Wales
, while a yellow wind warning started in Northern Ireland at 10:00
Amber warnings for wind in
northern England, Scotland, and parts of Northern Ireland
begin at 21:00
Ferry services in the Irish Sea are cancelled,
and there are also cancellations on the
CalMac service
around the west coast of Scotland
Tens of thousands of properties lost power in south-west England on Friday -
thousands are still waiting to be reconnected on Saturday

UK weather warnings: What you need to know
published at 11:12 BST
11:12 BST
When dangerous weather is forecast, a weather warning will be issued by the Met Office, the UK’s national weather service.
Weather warnings are given a colour – yellow, amber or red - with yellow being the lowest, and red the most serious. The colour assigned depends on a combination of two things: the impact the weather is likely to have and the likelihood of it happening.
Yellow warnings:
Are the ones you will see most often. They give you a heads up that severe weather is possible and to start planning for impacts to either travel, power or property
Amber warnings:
Mean travel disruption is more likely and there is a potential risk to life and property
Red warnings:
These are rare, and have only been issued a handful of times in recent years. They mean the Met Office believes that dangerous, potentially life-threatening weather is expected imminently and you should immediately take action to keep yourself and other safe
Image caption,
An example of a Met Office warning matrix. Here, the position of the tick indicates that a yellow weather warning would be issued

Yellow rain warning kicks in over Wales and large parts of England
published at 11:00 BST
11:00 BST
Breaking
It's now 11:00 BST which means the second weather warning has just taken effect - a yellow rain warning covering large swathes of the country.
Affected areas include the south-east, north-west England, south-west England, Wales, the West Midlands and Yorkshire and Humber.
The warning remains in place until 23:00 tonight.
The Met Office says to expect spray and flooding on roads, travel disruption and possible power cuts. It says flooding of some homes and businesses is also possible.
As a reminder: In an hour's time, a third warning will kick in - this time a yellow wind warning over Scotland and parts of England and Wales

'Hazardous' road conditions expected in Scotland, as drivers encouraged to delay journeys
published at 10:50 BST
10:50 BST
Police in Scotland has issued some travel advice ahead of Storm Boelo, with officials warning of "hazardous" conditions and a "high risk of disruption on the road network".
"Our advice is to plan ahead and consider if your journey is really necessary or if it can be delayed until conditions improve," says Supt Andy Barclay.
"Stopping distances can be at least double on wet roads compared to dry conditions, and spray can reduce driver visibility."
HGV and bus drivers have been told to drive with "extreme caution" and are being told they might be asked to park in a "suitable position" by the police.

Disruption expected across Scotland
published at 10:36 BST
10:36 BST
Graham Fraser
BBC Scotland News
Image source,
JulieBee/BBC Weather Watchers
Image caption,
It's already looking rather grey in North Ayrshire this morning
An amber weather warning is in place for the whole of mainland Scotland and the Western Isles from 21:00 tonight until 21:00 on Sunday.
The Met Office says flying debris caused by very strong winds of up to 80mph could cause injuries, while there is a chance of power cuts and damage to buildings.
The strongest winds will initially affect the west of Scotland - probably around the Western Isles and the coasts or Argyll - and the storm will then travel eastwards through Sunday.
Transport Scotland has said road, rail, air and ferry services are all likely to be affected by the conditions.
At the time of writing, 14 ferry services from CalMac have been cancelled. Anyone planning on travelling this weekend is urged to check before leaving home.

Irish Sea ferry crossings cancelled as Storm Boelo hits
published at 10:23 BST
10:23 BST
Ralph Hewitt
BBC News NI
Image source,
Getty Images
Sailings between Belfast, Liverpool and Cairnryan, near Stranraer, have been cancelled today, as well as those from Dublin and Holyhead, due to the bad weather.
The Met Office has a yellow weather warning for wind across Northern Ireland which started at 10:00 BST, while the north coast of the country will be placed under an amber warning from 21:00.
Meanwhile, the Republic of Ireland’s meteorological service Met Éireann has issued several Status Yellow and Orange wind warnings for a number of counties.
Belfast International Airport and Dublin Airport are advising passengers to check with their airline for the latest status of their flight.
In
preparation for the storm
, Northern Ireland’s Department of Infrastructure has said their teams have been checking and clearing road gullies, monitoring river levels and tidal surges, and deploying a portion of temporary flood defences.
You can read more about the warnings in place for Northern Ireland
in our story

As Storm Boelo hits UK, thousands still without power after Austen
published at 10:16 BST
10:16 BST
Storm Boelo is beginning to bring heavy winds and rain to the UK - but thousands of people are still being affected by Storm Austen, which arrived on Friday.
As of 09:45 BST,
5,774 properties
in England and Wales have power cuts.
The majority are in south-west England - the area most affected by Austen yesterday.
Image caption,
This National Grid map shows the location of power cuts - orange markers represent a singe "incident" (usually involving multiple properties), while blue circles represent multiple incidents

Yellow wind warning kicks in for Northern Ireland
published at 10:00 BST
10:00 BST
It's 10:00, which means the yellow wind warning over Northern Ireland is now in effect.
It will remain in place until 12:00 tomorrow.
In an hour's time, a yellow rain warning will also come into effect across Wales and large parts of England.
According to the Met Office, a yellow warning for wind means people should:
"Prepare to protect your property and people from injury. Check for loose items outside your home and plan how you could secure them. Items include: bins, garden furniture, trampolines, tents, sheds, and fences."

More on the new weather warnings from the Met Office
published at 09:34 BST
09:34 BST
We can now bring you more details on the two new weather warnings issued by the Met Office.
Amber wind warning:
This is in place in north-west Northern Ireland from 21:00 BST today to 10:00 tomorrow, impacting Antrim and Londonderry. The wind warning issued previously for Scotland has been extended south across northern England into northern Wales - it will kick in at 21:00.
Yellow rain warning:
This is in place from 11:00 to 23:00 today. It affects Wales and large parts of England, including the South East, the North West, the South West, the West Midlands and Yorkshire and Humber.
These are in addition to the three wind warnings (two yellow and one amber) that were
already in place
.

Flooding expected in Scarborough and part of Staffordshire
published at 09:13 BST
09:13 BST
Image source,
mrbyorkshire/BBC Weather Watchers
Image caption,
The Environment Agency warns further flooding is "expected" in Scarborough later today. For now, there's little cloud in the sky
Three flood warnings and 14 flood alerts are in place across England - a flood warning indicates flooding is "expected", while an alert means it is "possible".
Flooding expected
At
Foreshore Road in Scarborough
, where high tides
already caused flooding on Friday evening
- leaving some vehicles stranded and forcing roads to close
High tides were also expected to cause flooding at
Sandside in Scarborough
and people are encouraged to avoid coastal roads, footpaths and carparks at both locations
From yesterday evening, rising river levels were expected to cause flooding at
Saredon Brook in Standeford
, an area in Staffordshire
Flooding possible
Coastal areas of Seaford seafront
Hunstanton coast in Norfolk
North Sea coast from Whitby to Filey
River Alt, Formby to Huyton
River Cole, Dorcan Brook and South Marston Brook
River Maun in Nottinghamshire
River Sow and River Penk
Somerset coast at Porlock Weir
Parts of Stoke on Trent
Parts on Stone in Staffordshire
The tidal River Waveney from Ellingham to Breydon Water
The tidal River Yare from Thorpe St Andrew to Breydon Water
Upper Tame
Upper Tame at Sandwell Valley

When do we see the most named storms?
published at 08:14 BST
08:14 BST
Chris Fawkes
BBC Weather presenter
Image source,
BBC Weather
Image caption,
The winter months of December, January and February typically produce the highest number of UK storms
Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer.
The only month with no named storms in the eleven years that we've been naming storms in the UK is May.
The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months.
This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.
In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.

How to prepare for power cuts
published at 07:43 BST
07:43 BST
Image source,
Getty Images
As well as travel disruptions being expected from Storm Boelo, some properties in
areas under warning
could be left without power.
Power cuts can plunge communities into darkness and stop usual services from working, but here are some helpful tips on how to navigate an outage:
Candles and torches
can replace lights during power cuts, although it's important to remember naked flames can pose a fire risk
Keep cash on hand
as
shops may not accept phone and card payments when the power is out
Tinned food and gas stoves
will help keep you fed as microwaves, air fryers and some hobs and ovens demand electricity
Powerbanks
can help keep your phone charged, allowing you to see the latest updates
You can
report a power cut online,
,
external
or by calling 105, which is a free service in England, Scotland and Wales.

Hundreds of properties still without power in south-west England
published at 07:30 BST
07:30 BST
Hundreds of homes and businesses are still without power after Storm Austen battered parts of the country yesterday.
National Grid's map shows a concentration of power cuts in south-west England, the area worst affected by the storm.
In Cornwall, one incident near Truro has left 478 properties without power, while another near Penryn is affecting 127 properties.
One incident in Dorset is impacting 141 properties, with another 85 properties in Exmoor still without power. Both of these are not estimated to be resolved until 22:00 tonight, according to National Grid's website.
These are just a few examples from the swarm of red and blue incident dots seen on the map.
Image source,
National Grid

Storm Boelo expected to cause widespread travel disruption across Scotland and north of England
published at 07:15 BST
07:15 BST
Image source,
Getty Images
Image caption,
ScotRail says speed restrictions will be in place on some routes, with some services not running and cancellations possible as Storm Boelo hits
National Rail is warning that Storm Boelo may impact journeys and encouraging people to check before they travel.
It says:
TransPennine Express
is advising against anything but essential travel today and on Sunday - while there are no planned changes to the timetable today, speed restrictions will be in place across Scotland. Widespread disruption is expected on Sunday
Avanti West Coast
is advising people to avoid travelling north of Preston on Sunday
LNER
is advising against travel between Edinburgh and Aberdeen on Sunday
Northern
will see a reduction in the number of trains operating on several routes today
Speed restrictions will be in place on certain
ScotRail
routes today, some services will not run and there will be cancellations of revisions across the entire network from 21:00 tonight -
we've got more on Scottish travel disruption here
CrossCountry
says services travelling to or from areas north of Newcastle will face a speed restriction today and tomorrow
Although there is no Met Office weather warning over Wales today,
Transport for Wales
is warning of weather-related disruption to its network - Wales was hit by Storm Austen yesterday
Services in other parts of the country including
Great Western
are also warning there could be ongoing disruption today because of Storm Austen.

Is it unusual to see two storms so close together?
published at 07:02 BST
07:02 BST
Chris Fawkes
BBC Weather presenter
It's not unusual to get storms so close together, in fact they quite often arrive in clusters.
A strong jet stream
is needed to rapidly develop powerful wind storms. The process of creating such storms involves shifting warmer air northwards and cooler air southwards across vast areas of the Atlantic.
These temperature contrasts can provide a fertile environment for new low pressure systems to develop and if these subsequently get steered beneath a developmental area of a powerful jet stream, they can rapidly develop to create a new named storm with damaging winds.

How much disruption was caused by Storm Austen
published at 06:50 BST
06:50 BST
Image source,
Reuters
Storm Austen caused major disruption across parts of England and Wales on Friday - here's a recap:
Thousands of homes
were left without power, and gusts of up to 84mph (135km/h) were recorded in Jersey
In Brighton, dramatic footage captured the
collapse of part of the iconic West Pier
as it fell into the sea
All schools on Jersey and Guernsey closed
for the day and some in Cornwall were closed or started later than normal
Transport was also disrupted,
with some ferry services between the UK and France cancelled and trains cancelled and delayed
Jersey Airport said
flights
wouldn't be running until at least 17:00 on Friday, while departure boards at Exeter airport also showed multiple cancellations
Image source,
Russ Slater
Image caption,
The damage caused to a car hit by a tree in Horsham, West Sussex, on Friday
